reviews.quote: over the hill is a game that makes you fall in love with it. It challenges you without passing judgment. It gives you freedom while still guiding you through the desire to upgrade your car, and it rewards you whenever you discover something interesting on the map. Above all, Over the Hill is a game brimming with a love for the automotive world—a passion infused into every single polygon.

Over the Hill builds on Art of Rally’s tactile driving and distils the appeal of Saber Interactive’s complex off-roading sims into something much more approachable. The cute animal photography is the cherry on top.

over the hill is a peaceful sandbox game that gives you the freedom to do whatever you want to do. You can play with friends, roam the sandbox together while checking off objectives, or just enjoy your time in the cozy world. Playing alone can make the world feel a bit empty; it still has some kinks to work out, but there’s a very good time to be had just driving around and listening to the radio while you watch the sunset from a peak you just climbed.

The game's performance has been good; while it ran smoothly almost the entire time during our tests on a high-end rig, we do not expect it to perform as well on low-end PCs, given its significant RAM usage.

A few quality-of-life issues could use some work, but otherwise, over the hill reaffirms Funselektor’s knack for creating unusual and engaging driving experiences. Off-roading through the mountains isn’t for everyone, yet the Canadian studio’s latest manages to be accessible to newcomers, offering co-op sessions that can go on for hours without a hitch. If trekking through picturesque landscapes sounds appealing, over the hill will welcome you with open arms.

Ultimately, Over the Hill is a lovely little adventure that understands the simple joy of heading out into the wilderness and seeing what you stumble across. For me, it’s at its best when you’re tackling its trickier trails with friends, where a seemingly straightforward expedition can quickly descend into a chaotic and often hilarious rescue mission where you’ll be eating popcorn by the bucket-load. Progression could do with a little fine-tuning, and I personally don’t find solo play to have quite have the same appeal as multiplayer, but regardless – there’s a lot to like here. If you like the idea of going it alone, or if you’ve got a few friends willing to pile into their 4x4s and head up the trail with you, Over the Hill is well worth the trip.

over the hill offers a fun, easy-going offroading experience. But while I had a good time tackling the terrain both solo and with friends, there’s not a lot to do besides in the beautiful but barren environments. Future updates and DLC may eventually breathe more life into it, but until then over the hill remains a very casual experience that’ll only keep you occupied for brief stints.

While some players may find plenty of enjoyment in over the hill, its multiplayer adds little to the experience. The game looks peaceful, its simplistic art style is charming and the soundtrack fits the intended atmosphere, but frustrating exploration and underwhelming rewards quickly ruin that sense of tranquillity. Bumper Christmas lights are pretty funny, but not when you’ve tumbled down a hill thirty-seven times just to get them.

Almost the anti-driving game. Over The Hill is slow, laborious, and frequently frustrating. The vast game areas are adequately detailed yet oddly empty-feeling. While the expertly curated trial routes are standouts, you're essentially perpetually playing the worst bits of every open world driving game again and again, with little sense of variety or reward.

It's a game gloriously devoid of feature creep or noise, of time limits or competition: a refreshing, head-clearing space. In its quietly rugged way, it's the perfect cozy game. You watch your valiant little 4x4 crawl and bounce across a luscious wilderness as the sun rises and ambient guitar music wafts through the speakers and feel your heart fill with a kind of entranced patience. There's no rush. You'll get there in the end.

Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 serves as an ideal sequel to an already stellar game by refining the things that matter, dropping the things that don’t, and focusing on vastly expanding the blisteringly fast-paced, brutal action.

Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 not only refines what made the first game good, it polishes out the rough edges, adds more enemies, improves boss fights, brings stronger, grander, more interactive level design, and overall, more 40K. Whether you were a fan of the first Boltgun or diving in now, you're in for a treat.

If you want something you can jump into for a quick gameplay session and have an incredible time blasting through colorful stages and fiendish foes, look no further. Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 delivers fast-paced, exhilarating action that’ll get your heart pumping and your feet stomping. This game gives you that satisfying hit of nostalgia, but with a modern twist that feels charming and unique. With slick gunplay, a brilliant soundtrack, and dozens of tight levels, this is one you won't want to miss.

Warhammer 40K: Boltgun 2 is bigger and more ambitious than the 2023 original, with a new character, more enemies, weapons and places to go in the non-linear campaign. It remains a highly effective homage to classic boomer shooters and Warhammer 40,000. However, while the battles are bigger and more chaotic, there aren’t many changes of pace and the relentless action becomes a bit repetitive if played too long. Still, it’s hard not to recommend Warhammer 40K: Boltgun 2 for fans of retro shooters or Games Workshop’s beloved franchise.

Boltgun 2 is a confident, fast-as-hell, modern boomer shooter. With plenty of different ways to purge, fans of the genre will love to embark on a purge fest as either killing machine Malum Caedo or newcomer Nyra Veyrath, Sister of Battle, who is more of a space ninja. The game’s level design and pixelated vistas are particularly impressive. Without overstaying its welcome, Boltgun 2 is a gory, pixel-styled burst of adrenaline, cut into fun, bite-sized missions.

A nurgling genocide of a sequel that directly addresses almost everything that held the first game back, while still finding time to squeeze in a generous dollop of additional creativity. The best ‘90s FPS you never played.
Warhammer 40K: Boltgun 2 is a solid sequel to a flawed original. It fixes my main issue, with smartly designed levels that help you feel like a proper badass.

Warhammer 40K: Boltgun 2 firmly establishes itself in the old-school essence of the boomer shooter genre. By introducing a branching campaign structure, heightened verticality in level design, and two playable protagonists with distinct combat styles, the sequel evolves its visceral gameplay, even as it stumbles by setting aside the narrative weight and cinematics of the original title.

Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 refines what made the first game fun by adding a greater variety of enemies and weapons, and a second, very fun playable character. If you're in the mood for an old-school-style, ultra-violent FPS (and don't mind dealing with dumb enemy AI), Boltgun 2 is for you.

Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 carries the torch of the original, amplifying its exhilarating gameplay with a compelling new character, detailed enemy and world designs, and level branches that offer a surprising touch of complexity in their objectives. Technical hiccups can lead to moments of frustration that may stunt progress or the flow of action in a few ways. However, the snappy pacing helps keep things moving and context-specific character barks inject personality to round out the gore-geous mess you make in battle. Whether you're a Warhammer die-hard, a classic shooter fan, or simply boomer shooter curious, Boltgun 2 is a genuine blast and well worth your time.

Planet Zoo 2 raises the bar for the simulation genre, with new features and quality-of-life tweaks making the latest Frontier Developments title not only as the kings of the jungle, but also conquerors of the sea and the air.
Most importantly, every creature feels well-designed and well-thought-out. They don’t behave the same, and I lost so many hours simply observing what my favorite inhabitants were up to.

With lovely visual upgrades to its sprawling roster of land, air, and sea-dwelling animals and exciting expanded mechanics, Planet Zoo 2 is a vibrant and thriving sequel. I wasn't absolutely awed by all of the new stuff, and in particular I think wildlife reserves could be a lot richer than they are. But with plenty of management features to challenge my strategy-loving side and endlessly flexible building tools to inspire my creative side, there's not a lot more I could ask for. It's a roaring success.
Planet Zoo 2 isn’t a revolution, but it doesn’t need to be. It takes what made the original great and improves upon it in every way.

It's safe to say that Planet Zoo 2 is Frontier's biggest and best game yet. It looks fantastic, has a huge range of animals, and its greater focus on conservation makes for a wholesome and rewarding experience. There's a learning curve involved, though, so be prepared to put in the time if you want to get the most out of this wonderful sim.

Planet Zoo 2 is a stupendous upgrade over Frontier's first effort from 2019. The improvements made to the animal AI pathing, zoo customization and the new habitats areastounding. Frontier has made tremendous strides in this sequel, and while it may feel overwhelming to new players even with its comprehensive story mode, it may be a bit too much all at once in some places. That being said, absolutely nothing should stop you from taking the plunge into this spectacular zoo management simulation.

Planet Zoo 2 is, in my opinion, one of the best management sims ever made. The level of detail in not just the animals, but also the technical details and real-world education provided is like no other. It's so easy to lose yourself in a zoo, creating the perfect habitats for the amazing animals and truly feeling responsible for them and their well-being. The addition of aviaries and aquariums is a welcome one, and it's incredibly enjoyable to have the option to turn off the UI, go into a cinematic mode and simply watch the animals do their thing.
The fantastic aquariums and aviaries make Planet Zoo 2 the ultimate zoo simulator, though quite a few animals from multiple continents are still needed to make that dream complete.

Planet Zoo 2 is an engaging and rewarding management sim with gorgeous animal models and animations, alongside remarkable creative freedom. Despite a few shortcomings, some of which it has inherited from its predecessor, it is an excellent choice for players who love detailed management, though those primarily seeking a relaxing experience with animals may find it overwhelming.
Quotation forthcoming.

Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition is an accessible and modern experience that draws new players into the struggle to unify Japan for the first time, while allowing longtime fans to rediscover this beloved game. Those approaching Creative Assembly’s title for the first time can experience that entire historical period from start to finish, from the rise of the samurai to their fall, thanks to the inclusion of the Rise of the Samurai and Fall of the Samurai expansions. Veterans, on the other hand, will find a game with restored graphics and many quality-of-life improvements to the gameplay. Total War: Shogun 2 remains a masterpiece of the strategy genre to this day, and this new Complete Edition gives us yet another excuse to fight for the shogunate.

It's a spectacular, enormous experience that strategy fans will undoubtedly be happy to play for hundreds of hours, and it should serve as the definitive introduction to the series for new fans moving forward. Is it the best Total War game of all time? Though I definitely have a soft spot for the original Rome release, it's fair to say that this is just about as good as it gets in the genre.

The new edition corrects high-resolution interface issues, modernizes controls, adds the option to adjust settings in the Divided Kingdom, and includes important current graphical features. Total War: SHOGUN 2 - Complete Edition makes it easy to return to one of the best campaigns in the series.

Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition crafts a deep experience. It serves its grand strategy far better than its RTS combat, making enjoyment depend on which side of the gameplay you are mostly looking forward to.

Total War: Shogun 2 Complete Edition is something I’m absolutely thrilled to have in my life. I looked at it with rose-coloured sake glasses, and it did not disappoint. This is every bit the experience I recall from half a lifetime ago, with a new coat of ukiyo-e paint. The new visuals are absolutely stunning and bring one of the Total War franchise’s quintessential titles into modernity. I like to think I am a master of the new tactical features, but I fear that is far from the truth. This is a great “Complete Edition” for fans and newcomers alike.

Valor Mortis is the kind of ambitious swing that soulslike fans have dreamed of for years. Witnessing the horrors of war through William’s eyes is one of the best stories brought to the genre in recent memory, and its dark setting of an alternate 19th century Europe carries as much weight as the narrative itself.

The perfect soulslike doesn't exist. There's no such thing, and after so many years of playing them, I'm absolutely sure of it. All of them are bound by shared metroidvania design philosophies and incapacitating issues, and no matter how hard they try, they can never truly surmount them. But Valor Mortis certainly comes dangerously close to doing so, and with gameplay so fluid and a world so fascinating, it's basically as good as they come.

Valor Mortis rarely wastes a beat, producing a surprisingly powerful tale of barbarity that portrays the brutality of war not just through its vicious combat, but through the memory of those who never stood a chance of survival.

Although there is some room for improvement when it comes to refining a few of the technical aspects of the game, Valor Mortis is still a thoroughly engaging experience that left me more than satisfied with my time going through its story and learning about its world. I’m absolutely ecstatic to see what else One More Level has in store for Valor Mortis, and I will definitely be one of the first in line to return for its promised story expansion and New Game+ mode.
Valor Mortis stands out in a saturated genre thanks to its fun combat, excellent level design, and gorgeous visuals.

Valor Mortis is a solid title that kept me hooked for a 20-hour playthrough, delivering a rollercoaster of emotions along the way. To me, that is exactly why Soulslikes have become so popular. The "all-or-nothing" gameplay, high-octane and spectacular combat, and an intriguing setting make this game a standout in the genre, offering a fresh take on a formula that had long since stagnated.

Rather than merely borrowing ideas—from Dark Souls and Dishonored to Sunset Overdrive and even Frogger—One More Level blends them with their own strengths and an original setting to create something truly unique.

Valor Mortis delivers a tense and satisfying first-person soulslike experience, combining strategic combat, rewarding exploration, and a distinctive Napoleonic horror setting. Despite a few technical issues and uneven boss encounters, its strong atmosphere and cohesive mechanics make it a memorable adventure.
Featuring buttery smooth play, fans of first-person melee filled with impactful and meaty combat shouldn't hesitate to check out Valor Mortis.
Valor Mortis is a well-realised Soulslike FPS with a 19th-century coat of paint that enthusiasts of the genre will surely enjoy.

What surprised me most about Allogloom is how much it reminded me of the point-and-click games I played when I was younger, without ever feeling childish. A straight line runs from the curiosity that made me click everything in Putt-Putt, Pajama Sam, or Freddi Fish to the curiosity that kept pulling me deeper into Gruesome Grove and the world around it. The difference is what waits on the other side of the click. Those childhood games rewarded curiosity with jokes, animations, and friendly characters; Allogloom sometimes rewards it with something you probably wish you didn’t know, and I mean that as a compliment. Perhaps that’s why the comparison to those childhood adventures feels so correct. Allogloom feels like the genre grew up alongside the people who played them. The curiosity is still there, as are the strange characters and the inventory full of seemingly useless nonsense, but the questions are different now, and the answers can be considerably more uncomfortable. It reminded me why I used to click on absolutely everything in Putt-Putt, Pajama Sam, and Freddi Fish, without ever wanting to replay any of those games. We’re older now, and the moths grew up with us. Allogloom is definitely one of those point-and-click games I’ll recommend for years to come.
Allogloom is a beautiful, short game with an amazing, twisted art style, deep lore, and simple yet fun puzzles.

For those who want a neatly packaged, slightly eerie, yet beautiful escape to another world, Allogloom is amazing. If anything, I wish I could’ve had just a little bit more about the spaces we visit to see what was happening in each area. Again, this isn’t anything that’s a true negative, but I did end up with just a few questions on some of the areas we find ourselves. I want to learn more about the settings that have been created for Nora. The areas she finds herself in all seem to have their own reasons for being and I’d want just a little more to understand why. But even without this, Allogloom is a game worth your time if you want a bit of horror with your point and click games.
A macabre take on other worlds and how one perceives reality, Allogloom is a creepy-cute point-and-click treat for fans of haunting tales.

In its logic strings, Aloogloom is so satisfying. There’s victory in discovering exactly which item works with another, and that’s what all good point-and-click adventures should aspire to achieve. Pair this system with Allogloom‘s lush, moody artwork and its layered, macabre themes, and it’s an entirely unique experience that is rich and beautiful in approach. It’s a very strong debut from developer Galactic Ghosty, and one that deserves your attention.

Truckful offers a relaxing yet occasionally tense driving experience, combining package deliveries with a mysterious story, side missions, and collectibles. Its engaging narrative and puzzle-based gameplay make exploring enjoyable, although judging the depth of the environment can sometimes be difficult. Despite some grindy Scrap collecting, Truckful delivers a unique and compact adventure.

Truckful is a strange delivery game that shines in its genre mix, blending horror with cozy exploration. However, it also has plenty of speed bumps in its controls and exploration, creating a frustrating driving experience that could use more quality-of-life improvements. Still, once you get past those roadblocks, the game becomes surprisingly heartfelt, with a compelling story and a charming cast of NPCs who stick with you as you unravel the town's mysteries. It’s a bumpy ride, but if you’re willing to stick with it, Truckful is worth taking for a spin.

Truckful‘s flow might be interrupted by frequent loading screens, but it is otherwise a pretty fun, relaxing physics-puzzle about driving through a beautiful countryside delivering packages. That is, until sudden, unexpected but much-appreciated horror elements show up, giving the game a unique and threatening element not present in similar titles.

Truckful has a surprisingly deep, dark story with a lot of enjoyable, entertaining characters. This carried me through the game more than I expected, and I’m glad I got to experience what it had to offer. The physics are hit or miss depending on your driving, but the core mechanics and handling are fun. The game excels in story, world-building, mystery, and, more often than not, the main gameplay loop.

In the long run—much like any video game that simulates a job—Truckful turns into a routine: you end up doing the same things and, for the most part, driving the same roads. You move from one character to another, sometimes just to update them on the situation before speeding off to the next conversation. Car chases become few and far between—save for the showdown with the two ghosts—and the entire cargo-hauling mechanic tends to become monotonous. Ultimately, Truckful is a hard game to pin down: it aims to be "cozy" but fails, as the driving mechanics and camera angles will only frustrate you. It tries to be a thriller, yet that element becomes increasingly muted. It sets out to be a job-simulation game but embraces only the worst possible aspect of the job: the routine. The same faces, the same roads, the same packages—over and over again. At a certain point, you’ll even grow tired of the trees, the tree-lined roads, and the little birds.

I’m left feeling thoroughly satisfied with this grand new addition to a game I already loved. If you’re someone who’s been starving for Dragon’s Dogma content for a few years, then this is just about everything you were hoping for, and if you’re someone who bounced off the base game, then a lot of the more notable points of friction have been eased. Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is a tighter and more focused DLC that still manages to bring in very nearly everything about what made the base game such an incredible experience.
Dark Arisen has not only made Dragon’s Dogma 2 a must-play RPG, but it’s also one of Capcom’s best games in years.

Returning to Dragon's Dogma II is a treat in itself, but tack on a couple dozen hours of fantastic new content in a harsh but beautiful new region, and this is the best the game has ever been. Dark Arisen's unique loot cycle and challenging encounters work alongside a compelling new story to make it worth every penny.

If you love the idea of a grand fantasy adventure and experience a truly unique and immersive single-player game where you feel as if you’re actually accompanied by real players going on treacherous adventures together, with great moment-to-moment gameplay, then please, please play Dragon’s Dogma 2, then continue your adventure into Dark Arisen DLC and the cold lands of Norgan.

Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is often Capcom's open world RPG at its absolute peak. It's one hell of a meaty expansion, delivering a surprisingly involved story, joyous exploration, and deeply compelling combat. A transformative DLC.

Whether you’re a lapsed Arisen returning to the world of Dragon’s Dogma or a curious newcomer finally taking the plunge after Capcom’s stellar track record convinced you it was worth it, Dark Arisen proves to be an absolute delight. It builds upon the excellent foundation Capcom’s been polishing for the past two years, with sharp combat and engaging exploration. It challenges you with brutal new trials, all the while making the grind less unbearable. It cements Dragon’s Dogma 2 as an unforgettable experience.

Dragon’s Dogma II: Dark Arisen does what the original expansion had accomplished and set the bar with 20 hours more. With both Dark Arisen’s original premise and the Lost Rites challenges, there is more things to do, fight, and see, within the world even before deciding to end it at the finishing fight. While some things do remain the same from its 2024 base, the effort and vastness make up for it doesn’t demand a slow crawl, but a satisfying slow pain-and-gain run. For those who could tear themselves away from Crimson Desert, this Action RPG might be for you.

The Dark Arisen expansion for Dragon’s Dogma 2 adds a ton of new content to the base game, along with much-needed quality-of-life improvements that make the overall experience the most definitive one yet. If you enjoyed the base game, Dark Arisen is a must-play.

Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is an excellent expansion that builds on the base game's strongest elements while ironing out enough of the friction its weaker parts caused upon release. It advances the foundations of its exploration and combat loop, making it feel like the definitive version of those systems and something worth diving into right away.

Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is what expansions are truly about. The wholly distinct and dangerous region of Norgan sends players to explore the treacherous cold for new threats. What will be uncovered is a rich story, phenomenal encounters, and a wealth of new content that pushes Dragon’s Dogma 2 into the territory of an unforgettable journey.

To Nintendo fans who haven’t experienced Kingdom Hearts in its full splendor, this is an incredible time to jump in. These games are largely excellent action RPGs that are jam-packed with an out-there emotional story filled with oodles of Disney and Square Enix references.

This new collection cements the Nintendo Switch 2’s reputation as a great console for third-party ports, with a impressive array of games that look and run spectacularly even in handheld mode, particularly the most visually stunning of them all, Kingdom Hearts III.

Overall, Kingdom Hearts Collection 1-3 on Switch 2 is a fantastic package that is so close to being completely on par with the Integrum Masterpiece release. Kingdom Hearts 3 and A Fragmentary Passage’s framerate issues are the only things stopping it from definitively being my new favourite way to play, but the ability to go portable is worth those minor issues. Whether you’re a complete newcomer preparing for Kingdom Hearts 4 or a diehard fan like me looking for an excuse to replay, Kingdom Hearts Collection 1-3 on Switch 2 is a fantastic way to do it.

KINGDOM HEARTS Collection [I~III] is an ambitious, emotionally resonant package that highlights the series’ remarkable highs, messy experiments, and constant reinvention. Its native Switch 2 release finally fixes one of the franchise’s biggest accessibility problems, while Critical Mode, Re Mind, and years of updates make Kingdom Hearts III far stronger than it was at launch. However, uneven world design, inconsistent combat systems across entries, performance hiccups on Switch 2, and the continued absence of playable 358/2 Days, Re:coded, Melody of Memory, and the full χ saga prevent this from feeling truly definitive.

Kingdom Hearts Collection [I~III] is an excellent way to experience most of the Kingdom Hearts franchise, whether for the first time or for the umpteenth. Most of the bundled games deliver essentially perfect performance on the Nintendo Switch 2, while the more recent games still maintain consistent enough frame rates to please most. Being able to play the entire franchise on the go is a thrilling prospect, and I’ll likely be doing so for a good long while to come. This is a great way to get ready for Kingdom Hearts IV, and I’m sure many Nintendo-exclusive fans will be doing just that with this top-notch bundle.

Kingdom Hearts Collection [I～III] is an incredible package that brings nearly the entire saga together in one place. I would have liked to see a performance and frame rate toggle for Kingdom Hearts III, and the $75 asking price is a little steep considering how cheap this collection is on other platforms. At the end of the day, though, it’s Kingdom Hearts finally on Switch 2, and it’s hard to ask for much more.
KINGDOM HEARTS Collection (I-III) gives owners of the Nintendo Switch 2 a fantastic collection of games that all run superbly on the hardware. It is finally here!

Kingdom Hearts Collection [I–III] is the definitive collection of the series, offering everything fans need to know to prepare for the fourth numbered entry. A highlight is the Switch 2 version, which finally allows console owners to run the games natively and with good performance.

The Kingdom Hearts Collection [1~3] is the definitive way to experience the saga, offering polished ports and nearly the entire lore on Nintendo Switch 2. Despite minor performance dips, it’s the best entry point for newcomers and a nostalgic return for veterans.
KINGDOM HEARTS Collection [I~III] is a wonderful bundle of everything Kingdom Hearts, and on the Switch 2 it's just perfection.

Echo Weaver is a thrilling metroidbrainia that turns knowledge into progression, combining a tightly designed time loop with expressive platforming, rewarding exploration, and an engrossing mystery. Its abilities continually recontextualize the world and encourage experimentation, making repeat playthroughs especially compelling. A few minor progression quirks and the strict loop timer may not work for everyone, but Moonlight Kids delivers an inventive and deeply satisfying take on the metroidvania formula.

Echo Weaver is a very compelling concept for a Metroidvania, and presents some truly great gameplay ideas that I don’t think I’ve seen before. It’s a melding of various mechanics and while some of the resulting design choices make the game stumble just short of reaching excellence, the overall experience is one I can still see echoing in my brain for a long time to come.

Echo Weaver successfully blends story and time-manipulation gameplay into a "metroidBRAINia" experience—one where progress stems from the gradual acquisition of knowledge, mechanics, and abilities that were available all along, even if the player didn't realize it. Exploration via time loops is dynamic, and new discoveries are logged in an accessible, instructive way; however, the sheer number of shortcuts, techniques, and connections can eventually become mind-boggling, complicating the flow of this beautiful 2D platformer. The world itself is a massive puzzle, making the game recommended for those who enjoy unraveling the intricacies of its inner workings.

Echo Weaver’s unique approach to the Metroid structure is admirable, unique, and well executed. The sense of discovery is fantastic, and though I realistically probably won’t immediately play the game again, the idea that I could start with knowledge of basically all of the abilities to rip through the game at high speed is an enticing one. Developer Moonlight Kids puts a lot of trust in the player to figure out how it all works, and the reward is palpable. That trust leads to some frustrated, aimless wandering, and the platforming challenges occasionally venture into feeling unfair, but by the end you will feel like a genius. That’s a good feeling to leave a game with.

Echo Weaver is a bold take on the Metroidvania formula: a tightly constructed adventure that wholeheartedly commits to familiar science fiction elements and, in the process, makes them its own. Endlessly creative, sometimes frustrating, but always ingenious, it will worm its way into your brain and won’t let you go until you’re satisfied you’ve done everything it will let you. My advice is to play it today, with a few hours set aside for the first of several sessions that you’ll likely spend before you see and do everything. You’ll probably want them.

Neon Abyss 2 is a solid addition to today's indie roguelike scene. A cracking rogue-like shooter that builds on the solid foundation of the previous game, Neon Abyss 2 offers countless hours of frantic fun.

For better or for worse, Neon Abyss 2 feels very much like more Neon Abyss. But some meaningful changes in progression and permanent upgrades, along with a whole new way to play, make this zany roguelike just as gloriously addictive as the first game ever was.

Overall, I really enjoyed my time with Neon Abyss 2. It’s fun, easy to pick up and play, has a ton of progression systems to keep you hooked, and customization to make runs as easy or hard as you want. I would’ve loved more opportunities to create proper builds rather than having mostly incremental upgrades each run, which could have added an extra layer of complexity that the best-in-class games have.

Neon Abyss 2 is a beautiful sequel, with bolder visuals, flashier weapons and more game-breaking strategies. Unfortunately, the difficulty drops fast once you find the right item combination. The flashy gameplay is fun, but finding a game-breaking strategy happens a bit too quickly. The light show it creates is a joy to behold, yet I couldn’t shake the feeling that I, not the bosses, was the overpowered god of this neon world. A future patch could balance the item drops nicely. Neon Abyss 2 is a great continuation of the franchise that would benefit greatly from some balancing updates. For now, I’ll just go ahead and kill… kill… kill… as I mow through waves of enemies in the variety of game modes on offer. And maybe shoot some hoops with friends in between.

Order of the Sinking Star is a masterpiece. Its immaculate, mind-bending puzzles are perfectly designed to make you feel spectacularly stupid and then phenomenally smart. Its interconnected world, progressive revelation of layered mechanics, and post-credits continuation make it the ultimate Sokoban experience.

Order of the Sinking Star is a demanding and inventive puzzle adventure that constantly finds new ways to challenge your understanding of its rules. Its four distinct worlds, character-driven limitations, and increasingly intertwined mechanics make solving puzzles deeply satisfying, even if prolonged roadblocks can sometimes become exhausting.

Even after The Witness, Braid, and the many PuzzleScript games and Sokoban-likes that form its foundation, I'm sure I've never played anything to match. It’s not just a game of the year contender; fall in its clutches, Order of the Sinking Star might also end up the game you simply play the most, even—and most importantly—when you’re far away from the screen.

There’s no doubt that Order of the Sinking Star is one of the best puzzle games out there. The continual evolution of mechanics sprawling across a puzzle-ridden overworld is vast and exciting, and it’s so cool to see it all come from the same core concept. I like that it tells different stories within this, which leads to the bigger mystery of where we are to begin with. Sometimes it can feel a little overwhelming with every new mechanic introduced and then asked to apply, but it can also create some interesting scenarios that are enjoyable to play through.

Order of the Sinking Star is a massive, generous work full of discoveries, capable of reminding us that the best puzzle games aren't about finding a solution, but about learning to see the world in a different way.

Order of the Sinking Star is a massive and often brilliant puzzle game, built around the idea of constantly evolving rules that initially seem to have exhausted their potential. Its best moments come when different mechanics begin to interact, forcing players to rethink what they thought they had already learned. That same ambition can also weigh the experience down. With more than 1,400 puzzles, the sheer amount of content can sometimes feel excessive, while the difficulty occasionally depends more on remembering old rules than on finding an elegant solution. Even so, it remains an exceptional game for anyone looking for a demanding puzzle experience and willing to invest a considerable amount of time.

Order of the Sinking Star hands you more than a thousand handcrafted puzzles and no tutorials, and that trust makes it special. Intuitive character abilities, four distinct worlds, and a shared Overworld give every solution a sense of ownership, while undo and restart keep experimentation painless. The same philosophy backfires when progress stalls with no sign of what you missed, and the scale wears thin over long sessions. For patient problem-solvers, it is an excellent fit.

Order of the Sinking Star demands a lot from its players, but rewards them with plenty of variety through four distinct directions, each with its own mechanics, style and story. The lack of hints and increasing difficulty can be frustrating, especially for casual puzzlers, but the way the different systems come together in the Gold Rooms creates satisfying aha-moments. It is a game that trusts players to think for themselves, making it a rewarding challenge for puzzle enthusiasts.

Order of the Sinking Star is the most unique puzzle game I’ve ever encountered. Seemingly endless innovation and evolution of mechanics are just some of the key aspects of this game. While it doesn’t always hit the mark in terms of story delivery or length, it maintains its unusual gameplay throughout the many hours of gameplay. If you’re a fan of puzzles, then there’s never been a game more made for you.

Order of the Sinking Star might work better had it been a bit more curated in deploying its massive pile of puzzles, but the occasional frustration and overcomplication is an affordable price of admission to play around with so many fun ideas.

For their very first game, Wych Elm have blown it out of the park. I recommend Silver Pines to everyone: fans of horror, Metroidvanias, and detective stories. I even encourage those new to those genres to try it out, as it encapsulates a beautifully cinematic experience with a story you’ll want to uncover for yourself.

Silver Pines is a cerebrally divine love letter to David Lynch and all the narrative trademarks he was known for, from the cult classic Twin Peaks to Blue Velvet and Lost Highway. It digs even deeper to its spiritual successor Silent Hill, from the fog-filled streets to the nightmares that lurk with bared teeth, and embraces all those inspirations with the utmost grace and respect while still very much telling its own story. Combat can take a bit to get used to, but feels satisfying after a while with plenty of options at Walker's disposal. Meanwhile, the core investigation aspect of the game is well-executed if a bit unforgiving to the distracted player.

For their very first attempt, Wych Elm have knocked it out of the park. The influences from the masterworks of Lynch, Remedy and Silent Hill, the thriller steeped in ’90s Americana, the discovery of the city’s secrets, and that sense of unease and anticipation about what we’ll encounter every time we step into a new area, blended together in an unforgettable experience.

Silver Pines is a horror search-action game that borrows concepts from established games in the genre and uses them wonderfully to strengthen its own gameplay. The tanky controls and limited inventory kept me anxious as I tried to survive in this abandoned town, while the slowly unravelling story made me doubt whether Red Walker was as sane as he first seemed. The search for Eddie Velvet is a gaming experience that will haunt you like few other PI investigations can.

Compelling, atmospheric, and brilliant, Silver Pines is a dive into mystery that's hard to put down and even harder to let go. It makes you feel like a detective, an action hero, and a man on the brink of uncovering horrifying darkness all at once.

Silver Pines is a great survival-horror that came just at the perfect time. The story is intriguing, the atmosphere is gloomy and creepy, the puzzles are intricate and interesting, and the combat is decent and enjoyable. The minor missed steps with its story and aiming guns are easily forgiven when looking at the bigger picture, and it’s hard not to love it.

Silver Pines is an atmospheric game, a Metroidvania-style survival horror title that draws heavily from genre classics like Silent Hill, Resident Evil, and Alan Wake, as well as from television and film, such as Twin Peaks, The X-Files, and The Shining. However, these inspirations don’t reduce Wych Elm’s work to a mere collection of references; thanks to excellent storytelling, they allow the game to carve out its own path between nightmare and mystery. Solid gameplay underpins the experience, reinterpreting the genre’s conventions without forcing a radical overhaul. It’s also impossible not to mention the excellent art direction, featuring rotoscoped animations, and the soundtrack, with atmospheric music that heightens the tension. Silver Pines is a haunting adventure, a glimpse into the mystery of identity that straddles the line between reality and imagination.

Silver Pines is a glorious revival of the 90s survival horror formula. Fans of the early Silent Hill and Resident Evil games will be thrilled by a title that perfectly distills those classics' formulas, opting for 2D gameplay with strong Metroidvania elements.

Silver Pines is yet another excellent indie horror game and would not be out of place as part of the Silent Hill franchise. The combination of survival horror and more involved platforming exploration works fantastically well, while the town is chock-full of hidden secrets with enigmatic mysteries to solve.

Silver Pines is a sharp, moody debut. It mixes survival horror and Metroidvania design with real confidence. The hand-drawn art is gorgeous. All in all, the atmosphere is thick and unsettling. The mystery pulls you forward, and the world rewards curiosity. Combat feels stiff and lacks satisfaction. The game commits to old-school design. If you love atmospheric horror and don’t mind a slow burn, Silver Pines is a must-play this Halloween season.

The next tool you find is just barely within reach, and you will use it to create shortcuts and advance further. It definitely scratches the right spots to count as a Metroidvania (even though I really hate that term).

The puzzles are fun and while none so far have really had me scratching my head most have involved a very satisfying loop of item discovery, combination and reference to notes to solve. I especially like that you can take a photo of anything you want to see later, which makes some puzzles, such as remembering a radio's frequency and channel, very simple and they feel good to solve.

Most of the voice acting is top-notch, however I am very much not a fan that they cast an adult movie actor/youtuber as an NPC. Not only does it just conceptually bother me, but this person delivers a flat, sub-par performance. It never really ends well when they do this sort of thing (remember what's his name who was in Cyberpunk? Yeah neither does anyone else) and their performance here really is a D+ at best. Would have been much better off with an unknown.

Still, it can't take away that this is an inspired, thoughtful, and careful game. The people who made this actually cared about it and it shows. It is not the pinnacle of any of the genres it belongs to but it's very good and I'm happy to own it.

I was sold on Forever Ago from the trailer alone because I’m a sucker for these tear-jerking narrative experiences that happen to hit all the emotions. After being fully engrossed in Alfred's life, I know Third Shift has created something truly special. Forever Ago is an example of creative expression that the industry needs more of, and is definitely worth your time.

Forever Ago delivers a deeply moving narrative about aging, grief, and human connection, anchored by soulful voice performances and thoughtful presentation. Its pacing is deliberate, but as one of the most empathetic games of the year, it’s worth hitting the road for this scenic indie title.

Forever Ago is one of those games that left me feeling like I experienced something far greater than its short runtime suggests. Third Shift's debut title tells this genuinely heartfelt story about love, grief, and learning to move forward without leaving the past behind. The occasional technical hiccup is unfortunate, but it never overshadows what the game does so beautifully. Alfred's journey stuck with me long after the credits rolled, and I honestly didn't expect such a short road trip to emotionally sucker-punch me this hard. I know Forever Ago isn't perfect, but it's sincere, memorable, and easily one of the most affecting indie experiences I've played this year. Just be sure to hug your loved ones tonight and maybe call to check in on how they're doing, please.

Forever Ago is an intimate and moving narrative experience that handles complex themes like aging and loss with rare delicacy. Although its measured pace requires some patience, Third Shift’s title possesses all the warmth needed to win over anyone looking for a profound and reflective story.
Forever Ago is a beautiful tale of loss, grief and growth, and Arthur's roadtrip reminds us all that you just can't plan life.
Forever Ago takes you on an emotional journey to relive the life of a seemingly grumpy old man. It's impressive story-telling that will keep you immersed right through to the end.

Forever Ago is a celebration of life, a beautifully written road-trip on tragedy, love and healing. Despite its technical issues and lack of player agency, it's an example of how walking simulators create unique experiences.

Forever Ago is a quiet, somber yet hopeful exploration of grief, anchored by two wonderful performances in particular, that is unfortunately lacking from a gameplay perspective, but ultimately marks a solid debut for developer Third Shift.

Third Shift’s debut title, Forever Ago, is a remarkable achievement that takes a rare and courageous path in modern development by casting players as an elderly protagonist on a poignant journey through grief, redemption, and meaning, and against all odds, succeeds in crafting an experience that is as deeply reflective as it is charming and peaceful.

Forever Ago is a narrative experience that succeeds in how it handles its plot and prompts reflection on grief and the pain of loss. The gameplay could have explored the camera mechanics more, but the locations, memories, and people encountered along the journey offer moments of reflection and create a captivating experience.

An unexpected gem in almost every way. I don't think many were crying out for a Hellraiser game, but everyone will be demanding a sequel to Revival, as Saber's horror show delivers a compelling, rich journey through pain and pleasure.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival is a fantastic game that’ll satisfy both franchise and horror survival fans. Depending on whether or not you can stomach it, of course. It really doesn’t hold back, as it shouldn’t. Between the intense cinematics and the gut-wrenching narrative, this game pulls on every string. The Cenobites of Clive Barker’s world are known for two things: pain and pleasure. And this game showcases it all. There were many times when, while adventuring through the cultists’ underground lair, the world at large, or through the sex club, I had to scrape my jaw off the floor. It is a spectacle, and if you can handle a metric ton of body horror, this game should be on your radar.

Hellraiser: Revival is a faithful adaptation of the universe created by Clive Barker, combining an oppressive atmosphere, grotesque visuals, and genuinely tense moments with a structure heavily inspired by games of the genre, most notably Resident Evil 4 Remake. Although the puzzles are simple and the difficulty decreases considerably as the player masters its mechanics and abilities, the campaign manages to hold its own thanks to the excellent setting, intense chases, and creative use of the Lament Configuration. It's not revolutionary, but it's an interesting and authentic survival horror game for fans of the genre and, especially, of Hellraiser.

Those unfamiliar with Barker’s work who are looking for a strong title in this genre will find one that offers plenty of variety and a striking visual identity. It may not reinvent the wheel, but it knows how to combine its gameplay elements in a highly effective and engaging way.
Hellraiser: Revival is at its best when its horror gamification takes a back seat, providing a world that is equal parts depraved and disturbing, scary and thrilling.
Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival is not for those with weak stomachs. It's also got a lot of painful imagery. If you can power through that, there's a solid survival horror experience underneath.

I am pleasantly surprised at how much I enjoyed Hellraiser: Revival. Its respect for its source material is apparent throughout, with the Labyrinth, the Cenobites, and the Genesis Configuration being standout pieces of the puzzle. The rest of the game isn't reinventing the wheel for first-person horror, but the "don't fix what isn't broken" approach works just fine here. The squeamish need not apply, as there are moments made to make your skin crawl, but even the most horror-averse people can have a great time in this Labyrinth. Saber Interactive has such sights to show you, and thankfully, there's more pleasure than pain.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival delivers an excellent adaptation by expanding the franchise's mythology and book lore, bringing back the classic voice of Pinhead alongside a bold Unreal Engine 5 art direction. Although it stumbles confusedly between deliberate survival horror and action FPS, the title establishes itself as a worthy adaptation of the series' cultural impact.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival succeeds above all where it matters most: atmosphere, visual identity, and fidelity to the franchise’s aesthetic. The Genesis Configuration adds personality to a fairly traditional survival horror framework, though issues with balancing, AI, and protagonist writing hold back its potential. A successful adaptation, even if not without its rough edges.

It has some issues than can annoy, such as difficulty spikes and a couple of troublesome forced stealth sections, but these don't stop Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival from being a thrilling rollercoaster of a survival horror experience. Sexy, gory and grotesque are perhaps the best words to sum it up.

El misterio que rodea a los personajes, los cenobitas y los acontecimientos también está muy bien **** trabajo de voces está a gran nivel, destacando especialmente Doug Bradley como Pinhead, cuya interpretación es uno de los mejores elementos del **** historia es muy buena y cuenta con un guion bastante sólido. Mi principal crítica es que numerosos personajes advierten al protagonista de que ayudar a Sunny podría ser un error, pero él continúa haciéndolo sin cuestionarse seriamente sus intenciones. Esa falta de dudas hace que su comportamiento resulte algo forzado en determinados momentos.Gráficamente alcanza un nivel notable. Los modelados de los personajes son discretos, pero cumplen correctamente. Su verdadera fortaleza está en los escenarios, la dirección artística y la recreación del universo de Hellraiser. Además, es un juego claramente dirigido a un público adulto, con escenas muy fuertes, violencia explícita y un tono **** conjunto, es un survival horror muy recomendable, con una jugabilidad entretenida, excelentes enemigos, buena historia y una ambientación extraordinaria. L’histoire est excellente, le gameplay est solide et l’immersion est au rendez-vous. On retrouve une approche horrifique qui peut rappeler Resident Evil 7 ou Resident Evil Village, avec cette tension permanente, cette sensation de vulnérabilité et cette ambiance oppressante qui nous pousse à continuer malgré le malaise.

Mais ce que je respecte surtout, c’est que les développeurs ont osé quelque chose que peu de studios prendraient le risque de proposer aujourd’hui. Hellraiser n’est pas là pour plaire à tout le monde, et c’est justement ce qui fait sa force. Cet univers n’a jamais été Disney, et il n’a pas à le devenir ! C’est sombre, dérangeant, brutal et parfois franchement malsain. C’est précisément ce qu’on vient chercher quand on plonge dans l’univers des Cénobites.

Quant à certains testeurs dits professionnels qui descendent le jeu sans lui laisser la moindre chance, je me demande parfois s’ils connaissent réellement l’œuvre de Clive Barker et ce qui fait l’essence même de Hellraiser. On voit régulièrement des jeux encensés et surcotés recevoir des notes délirantes, alors qu’ici, lorsqu’un studio prend des risques et assume pleinement une identité aussi particulière, certains semblent soudain beaucoup moins indulgents.

Tout le monde a le droit de ne pas aimer, bien évidemment. Mais encore faut-il juger un jeu pour ce qu’il est, et non pour ce qu’on aurait voulu qu’il soit.

Pour environ 40 €, c’est une véritable pépite pour les fans d’horreur, de gore et de l’univers Hellraiser. Une proposition qui assume ses choix, respecte son identité et n’essaie pas de plaire à tout le monde.

Ma conclusion : si vous aimez Hellraiser, l'horreur viscérale, les ambiances macabres et les jeux qui osent sortir des sentiers battus, foncez ! Les Cénobites ne sont pas là pour vous faire des câlins. Ils sont là pour vous faire découvrir des sensations que vous n’êtes pas près d’oublier !

The Coalition has elevated the franchise to new heights, crafting an engaging, brutal, and surprisingly intimate campaign that’s full of smart gameplay mechanics and wonderful surprises. It’s the best Gears has ever felt to play, and the best it’s ever looked and sounded on the big screen. Gears of War: E-Day? It's a f.cking masterpiece.

Gears of War: E-Day is, for me, the best game in the series and The Coalition's finest work to date. Its campaign brings Marcus and Dom back without relying solely on nostalgia, delivering a darker and more brutal take on the origins of the Locust threat.

Gears of War: E-Day is a monumental triumph from a developer that irrefutably understands what’s important to fans: Gears isn’t just about tearing through Locust with a chainsaw, it’s about brotherhood, sacrifice, and grief. The Coalition has delivered an unforgettable campaign packed full of fresh ideas whilst staying true to what makes Gears so special. The Locust are back and more terrifying than ever, and blasting them to bits is incredibly satisfying. This is the best the combat has felt in twenty years, and fighting to survive the fall of Kalona will leave you speechless. Through its stunning locations, characters, and cinematics, E-Day is a visual powerhouse and one of the best-looking games I’ve ever seen on Xbox.

Weapons of all kinds, gadgets, and locations brimming with possibilities form the foundation of a story that excels in every aspect. Marcus and Dom return alongside old and new acquaintances in a prequel that feels fresh and invigorating. The story of Kalona’s downfall on E-Day serves as the starting point for a war-torn odyssey filled with unique situations, memorable scenes, and the feeling of experiencing an iconic moment in a saga that, for many, is a must-play. Gears of War: E-Day marks a turning point for the Xbox catalog with a console and PC exclusive that’s determined to raise the bar for Microsoft.
A campaign executed to perfection in terms of both technical aspects and gameplay. A brutal and intense war spectacle featuring the best Gears story to date.

I have to say that Gears of War: E-Day is an absolute triumph of a game. The maps in the multiplayer and the campaign are big, with things to find in unlikely corners. From there, exploration in the story mode should be seen as its own reward. This is a game full of content, and you’ll spend hours upon hours taking in everything it has to offer.  Whether you’re here for the campaign, or prefer to get invested in the multiplayer, if you have the slightest interest in Gears, you have to play Gears of War: E-Day. It really is that simple.

Gears of War: E-Day delivers arguably the franchise's finest, most atmospheric campaign, brilliantly balancing pulse-pounding action with genuine horror roots. By pairing breathtaking Series X visuals and refined combat with a deeply emotional return to Marcus and Dom, The Coalition has delivered a masterclass prequel that restores complete faith in Xbox's future. A triumph from start to finish.

Gears of War: E-Day shines by showing off humanity's perseverance. Every new character stands out, never overshadowed by the legacy of Marcus or Dom. Even with the game taking place in one city over several days, the evolution of that city and its inhabitants has created fleshed-out characters that you're rooting for the success of every step of the way.

E-Day succeeds in telling the story of Emergence Day in a gripping, desperate, and most importantly, fun way. The culmination of 20 years as a franchise, refining everything the series is into a must-play XBOX title that takes you on a gloriously brutal, emotionally-satisfying, and epic, cinematic adventure.

Gears of War: E-Day delivers arguably the series’ strongest campaign, combining mature, restrained storytelling with the return of Marcus Fenix’s charismatic presence. Already among the franchise’s finest entries, it could become a serious Game of the Year contender if its content-rich multiplayer matches the campaign’s quality. Regardless, Xbox players should not miss this outstanding return to form.

reviews.author: LancerPelican
reviews.quote:
What I liked: The city of Kalona and watching it fall and become utterly destroyed over the coarse of the campaign. Level design was nice. The gameplay was fun. The progression was good with weapon mods and upgrades. The overall plot of E-Day was great. Daan Riggs, the Kemara Twins and Tai Kaliso stood out the most as side characters. Horde Siege is very fun but could be further expanded upon in scale and depth. 

Why this game falls flat: Marcus and Dom do NOT feel like the leads at all. Especially if you 100% the campaign and experience everything the campaign and to offer the dialogues that are spoken within the main squad. The relationship between them doesn’t really change or grow until the very last chapter. Dom especially was written like a stale tomato and nothing like how he was in the first three games. Provides minimal commentary, some input here and there… that’s it. I’ve no clue how anyone could’ve approved writing a legacy franchise character like this and pushed this background role on him. Marcus too largely takes a backseat up until the very end as well. So who are the actual main focusses of the story? The Coalition new original character Mags Carter. What’s frustrating is not only the fact that she had a larger focus as you progress through the campaign but there’s absolutely nothing redeeming about her. She is so boring, uninteresting, and written like they are born of pessimism. Lucas isn’t great either. And just like Gears 4 and 5, the studio fails to write actual meaningful dialogue. In one section in the main campaign after defeating the frog like enemies, Lucas literally yells “well that was… something”. Are you fr? Another section in the final chapters after flipping a switch to cross a crane in the docks. AS THE PLATFORM IS TURNING IN FRONT OF YOU Mags has to let the player know “the platform is turning we should be able to cross” like no kidding thanks? Or during Act 3 while riding a sky train, after crashing and getting off she will say “always hated riding the train”. What is this man? But fine… fine if you want to ignore something like that because it’s a little nitpicky and incessant alright. But what you can’t ignore is their utterly dull personalities. Mags is constantly pessimistic. Always complaining and dumping her past experiences in the cog every chance she gets. When the cog soldiers on the bridge make fun of Lucas for being a by the book soldier she shoots it down and tells him to not listen to them everyone goes through it. Can we not make a joke? But in the same act proceeds to make fun him herself on many occasions lmao. This writing doesn’t add anything to the characters at all. I thought Lucas would be a character who gives us an outlook of E-Day through someone who’s never seen the horrors of the pendulum wars and war in general. At first it seemed to be going that way in Act 1 but went NO WHERE after that. He was desensitized to it all immediately and just asked basic questions here and there. A scene in act 4 also took a lot of seriousness out. We come to learn Lucas broke strict protocol and mentions how he wanted to experience being on the front lines of the Pendulum wars with his friends, so he decided to hold a prolonged communication with his old friends as they were fighting the UIR. Turns out the indies tracked the signal and they all died because of him. At first, you see how that experience really broke him. Understandable. But what utterly destroyed this scene was Mags coming in saying how “we all get it wrong.” SERIOUSLY LOL? Get it wrong lol? Writing like this just never felt like the game could be taken seriously. In act 3 Marcus tells Mags who he’s barely known for 2 days about the truth behind Carlos LMAO. 

The final fight was very average feeling like a modernized version of RAAMs fight in Gears 1, and the story overall felt rushed towards the end and didn’t really land. The open sections and acts 2-4 were also very bare bones. They were very detailed and looked stunning, but had no substance in them. The over abundance of hard cases all over these maps was very frustrating to grab and I don’t understand how anyone can find all of them without looking at a guide.

Overall, I feel like this game is best to play using gamepass or grab on sale. I cannot believe they charged $100 for a FOMO edition. Let alone the base $70 price tag. I do believe this game can be a solid foundation for what comes next as they’ve already built out a lot of what they would need for future installments. That is if the studio gets another shot after this. The Gears franchise has been in a niche corner for a LONG time. And with the creative decisions they’re making some good but still a lot more bad I don’t know who this franchise is for anymore. Newer audiences have no interest in Gears of War. And we can see that with data on the last three games. And the core audience seems to be fading as well. At this point just remake Gears 2 and let the franchise rest

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is everything I hoped it would be. Fuse built a campaign that keeps giving me reasons to master the tracks, then made the racing feel good enough that I wanted to. By the time I was done with the campaign, I found myself happy and whispering one thing to myself: Now this is podracing.

These worlds don't just look beautiful, from Jakku's dunes and wrecked Star Destroyers you must thread between to Crait's white crystalline surface with red dust billowing underneath. They're also carved up into fascinating tracks that blend tight underground corridors where cornering is a constant discussion with death, and daringly wide-open outside sections where I once got so turned around I ended up going backwards. These are places that constantly shift in the way that they challenge you, and I suspect that better racers than me will spend an awfully long time working out the optimal strategies for handling each one.

Star Wars Galactic Racer is a Star-Wars-authentic thrill rush that may be the best racer in a decade. It’s such a wonderful, engaging experience that literally does everything right. Just be warned – as a roguelite – the on-ramp can take time while presenting a higher difficulty level.

While the lack of local multiplayer is unfortunate, the decision to drop the mode so that the game is kept at a locked frame-rate is the right one. The game is so fast-paced that you need every millisecond possible. The tracks are all excellent, the music and sound effects are jaw-dropping, and both gameplay and customization have a ton of depth. The single player campaign is surprisingly good and has a lot more under the hood than I was expecting. Its roguelike elements are well-thought out, and will keep you coming back for more well after you beat the game. Online multiplayer has a variety of modes, from traditional arcade style races to entire tours across the galaxy, so that every type of player can find something to enjoy. Overall, Star Wars: Galactic Racer has just the right amount of nostalgia, and is a true evolution of the podracing experience. It’s frenetic, bombastic, and above all else, incredibly fun.

METACRITIC REVIEW | 10/10

I have been in the skies of Strangereal since Air Combat on the original PlayStation. I have completed every entry in the franchise. After 145 hours with Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, including achieving Platinum with the ultra rare Ace of Aces trophy requiring S rank on every mission at ACE difficulty, I can say without hesitation that Wings of Theve is the best Ace Combat game ever made. It surpasses Ace Combat 5: The Unsung War, which held that title for over two decades in my personal ranking.

Storyline

Project Aces has consistently delivered narratives that punch above the weight of what an aerial combat game should be capable of producing. Wings of Theve continues that tradition at the highest level the series has ever reached. The story respects franchise lore, advances the Strangereal timeline in a direction that has longtime fans watching the approach toward Ace Combat 3 Electrosphere territory with genuine excitement, and delivers emotional beats that land because the character work earns them. For players new to the series, it functions as a compelling standalone entry. For veterans who have followed Strangereal for decades, it rewards that investment meaningfully.

Gameplay

The moment to moment aerial combat is the most refined the series has delivered. The new control scheme is accessible for new players entering the franchise and represents a genuine design consideration for that audience. Veteran players who prefer the classic framework have Type B available and I returned to it immediately. Both work. The choice existing is the right decision.
The ACE difficulty S rank requirement is exactly what the series needed. This is not a participation trophy challenge. Clearing every mission including free missions at ACE with S rank demands genuine mechanical mastery of the aircraft, weapon systems, and mission design. The Ace of Aces trophy sitting at 0.3% rarity at time of writing reflects exactly how demanding that requirement is. It is the kind of challenge that justifies extended time investment and delivers genuine satisfaction when completed.

Music

Everflow and Hortus Regis Alti belong in the conversation for best tracks in the franchise's history, and Ace Combat's musical history is exceptional. The soundtrack as a whole is phenomenal and serves both the combat sequences and the narrative moments with the tonal precision the series has always delivered.

Technical Performance

Reviewed on base PS5, LG OLED G3 in Game Optimizer HGiG mode, and Samsung HW-Q990D in Game Mode Pro. The game performs beautifully on base hardware. The PS5 Pro Enhanced version likely elevates this further but the base experience is polished and visually strong throughout.

Content and Longevity

145 hours in and the Campaign Medal completions and online content still remain. The MRP grind for the 25,000,000 total required for trophy purposes alone represents substantial content engagement. The upcoming super aircraft DLCs are something I am genuinely looking forward to, as the franchise tradition of legendary aircraft additions has always extended the experience meaningfully.

For New and Returning Players

Wings of Theve works as both a franchise entry point and a veteran celebration. New players get a complete, compelling aerial combat experience with an accessible control option. Returning players get a love letter to everything that has made Strangereal one of gaming's most underappreciated fictional universes.

The AC3 Question

The timeline is approaching Electrosphere territory. Project Aces, if you are reading reviews: do not remaster. Remake. Ace Combat 3 deserves the full treatment and Wings of Theve has proven the team is capable of delivering it at the highest level.

10/10. The best Ace Combat game ever made. Essential for fans of the series and a genuine recommendation for anyone who has never played one. Get in the cockpit.

As a love letter to the immersive sim genre and a whole host of games that rank among my all-time top 20, RetroSpace is an absolute joy to play. The only real shame is that it never quite manages to rise above its inspirations, despite having all the ingredients to do so. [Issue#375, p.60]

RetroSpace brings back the philosophy of classic immersive sims inside a bizarre, satirical and distinctive retro-futuristic universe. Its freedom works because weapons, stealth, Mutamods and environmental interactions remain genuine options rather than mandatory solutions. Exploration is also its most divisive element: finding your way without waypoints can be genuinely rewarding, but the minimal map and deliberately vague directions can sometimes turn discovery into frustration.

RetroSpace puts humanity’s survival in the hands of a janitor, giving its System Shock-style adventure a blue-collar twist. Its environmental interactions and weird Mutamods make it a memorable trip, even if some inconsistent stealth, vague objectives, and some shaky portable PC performance sporadically get in the way.

If you can stomach Retro Space’s cloying satire, and its stifling beholdenment to classic immersive sims, you’ll find a game with sprawling, multilayered systems which smash together in amusing and novel ways.

Amid so many quick cash-ins that prey on nostalgia, this is a remaster done right. Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered is a fantastic modernisation that completely overhauls the visuals of the original game while adding smart new features and quality of life improvements, making it just as fun and enthralling as it was a quarter of a century ago.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered brings a PS2 legend to modern hardware with a complete technical overhaul, rock-solid frame rates, and its iconic cheesy voice acting left completely intact. While old-school map pacing and brutal archers show the game's age, optional modern dodge controls and deep co-op gameplay make it an absolute blast for nostalgia seekers.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered is old yet new—a trip down memory lane that’s pure nostalgia from the moment the game starts. It’s a title that never tries to be anything other than what it is, staying true to the essence that made the musou genre popular worldwide.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered is a faithful revival that preserves the slower, weightier combat, campy English voice acting, repeated campaigns, and split-screen chaos that defined the original. Its Unreal Engine 5 makeover and modest gameplay additions improve the experience without sanding away its old-school identity, though dated AI, repetition, and occasional technical issues may make it a tougher sell for newer Musou fans.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered is the first remaster of the Dynasty Warriors series from Koei Tecmo and Omega Force, and hopefully not the last. While musou games aren’t a groundbreaking genre in 2026, it’s fun to just hack and slash at cannon fodder as you try your best to complete the objective (usually to win). Though, it’s disappointing to see not many updates regarding accessibility features. Regardless, while the formula isn’t new, it’s great for those nostalgic fans and newcomers to the series.

Huge, often empty battlefields are still a chore to traverse, and mowing down hundreds of foes with the same three combos over and over again can be a big ask here in 2026. Still, with so many character stories, unlocks, and game modes to chew on, Remastered earns an easy recommendation if you're a Dynasty Warriors diehard — and I certainly wouldn't be against Koei Tecmo reviving the likes of Dynasty Warriors 4 and 5 in this style.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered brings the 25 year old classic hack-and-slash title back to life. Fresh lighting and overhauled visuals sparkle, while modern combat elements elevate the slicing and dicing nicely. While there's plenty to cut your teeth on here, the old frustrations with stun-locking enemies, less interesting mission designs and getting crossbow mobbed irk sooner than they should. At least the dialogue is absolutely hilarious and the series' charm remains fully intact.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered achieves its goal of breathing new life into a classic Dynasty Warriors experience, but with no changes to the gameplay, it soon begins to feel too basic and repetitive.

This remaster successfully modernizes a genre-defining classic with impressive visual updates, yet it remains anchored to twenty-five-year-old design limitations. While the simple, repetitive combat provides nostalgic satisfaction for veteran players, the experience inevitably pales in depth and mechanical complexity compared to more modern, refined entries in the series.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered brings back a true classic in a shiny Unreal Engine 5 coat, delivering an entertaining action game packed with content and a successful visual overhaul. However, it is very much a case of quantity over quality, as the repetitive levels, nonsensical story and lack of depth become increasingly hard to ignore, especially if you don't have nostalgia on your side. As a remaster of a 2001 classic it certainly succeeds, but don't expect any kind of revolution.

reviews.author: TachibanaLuiz
reviews.quote: When they announced Dynasty Warriors 3 Remastered, I was not sure if it was a remake or a remaster. We already knew from the trailers that they kept the same voices, cutscenes, and even the mispronounced names. But actually playing it made it completely clear that it is a pure remaster and not a remake, because everything else is exactly like the PS2 classic. They just gave it beautiful modern visuals. It perfectly captures that classic **** gameplay is way more fluid. Combos are fast, the new evasion mechanic is a lifesaver, and bows are actually useful now to stun enemies or snipe when your health is low. The classic difficulty is still brutal and the peons are aggressive. It is not one overpowered guy against a thousand weaklings, you have to fight for survival. Crowd control is mandatory and the morale system actually matters. You have to kill minor officers to boost your army. The Musou Guard system that lets you use main roster characters as bodyguards is also a great addition.Completing specific stage conditions to unlock items makes map exploration really engaging. There are plenty of great items to collect, and the fire arrows were easily my personal favorite. Another huge positive is that the roster is not fully unlocked right from the start. You actually have to trigger specific battlefield parameters to reveal and unlock the secret characters one by one. That sense of progression makes the game feel much more rewarding and pushes you to try out every single character just to see how they look revamped in Unreal Engine 5. The endgame grind is also awesome with Chaos mode, which is genuinely tough, but completely worth it if you want to hunt down the fifth weapons, the unique ultimate gear for each **** revamped maps look great, especially the snow and rain effects. I loved being able to explore more, like getting up on the castle walls. The original soundtrack is still flawless. The story has not changed, it is short, hypothetical, and definitely not the place to learn Three Kingdoms history. It keeps that goofy tone veterans love, though newcomers might be confused.Missions are repetitive, but that is just the DNA of the original game. It is completely different from DW Origins in combat and design, but honestly I had more fun with this.Still, it feels a bit like a prototype for future remasters. The biggest flaw is recycling generic NPCs from DW9 instead of keeping their classic designs. It does not ruin the game, but it is a missed opportunity.Versus mode is fun, but it really needs an offline bot option for those who just want to test things out. Still, the upcoming online mode update will be huge and should boost sales.There is something that bothered me a bit, which is the loading screens. When you are about to enter the map and start a battle, there are at least two loading screens and sometimes it takes a while. I am not sure if this happens because of the device I am playing on, the Steam Deck, or if the console versions also have this problem. It is an annoying thing that wastes some of your time, but it does not really ruin the overall experience. Speaking of the Steam Deck, in terms of performance, it runs at a solid 30 FPS on medium and high settings, only dropping slightly when the screen is absolutely packed.I hope this sells incredibly well. I want them to take notes and give us Samurai Warriors 2, Dynasty Warriors 5, and Warriors Orochi Z next!

Ultimately, Thank You, Bus Driver is not a full-fledged game in any traditional sense or price. What it actually is may be more important for them right now; an assertion of the passion and creativity that Double Fine have as a developer, no matter what the budget or timeframe. A few hours of chaotic fun delivered with signature charm; it’s more of an entertaining curio than anything else. Even so, it is small, but worthy addition to the Double Fine catalogue for fans of the studio and hopefully – a good sign of things to come.

Thank You Bus Driver delivers a quirky, charming spin on arcade driving with satisfying bus handling, chaotic passenger management, and an inventive 1950s cartoon aesthetic. Its roguelite progression and shifting rules create some entertaining runs, but limited variety, repetitive objectives, and an irritating soundtrack cause the novelty to wear thin long before the journey is over.
